correctness.rationale: The unsigned incidence matrix has full column rank, so all m facets and ridge pairs are genuine. The exact inverse tridiagonal Green formula and affine tangent-gradient projection establish H=G^{-1}-bb^T/t and every indexed cosine. Explicit positivity for same-parity entries and strict negativity for opposite parity establish the complete sign counts. The signed kernel ratio follows by parity-split Riemann sums; integrating the order-statistics triangle yields the claimed logarithmic CDF. The standalone checker independently compared exact affine and projected Gram constructions for m=3..15 (559 ridges), and numerical m=650 limit profiles; computations corroborate but do not substitute for the proof.

originality.rationale: The graph-edge simplex definition and tree-simplex property are classical (Tran–Ziegler), and the tridiagonal inverse is a classical ingredient. Neither inspected primary work nor the closest published geometric records states or implies the fully indexed ordinary path edge-simplex normal Gram, parity right-angle law and logarithmic signed kernel-ratio limit. The odd-cycle unsigned-edge theorem has a different matrix and uniform limit and therefore is not a stronger covering theorem. Historical priority is provisional due to incompleteness of indexed literature.
residual_risks: Equivalent historical facet-angle results might occur in unindexed simplex-geometry literature under a different name.
A generic all-simplex stochastic angle theorem with the same vertex Gram data, if found, could imply the limiting law; none inspected here covers it.

value.rationale: A complete natural metric invariant (every Euclidean ridge angle) of a graph-defined simplex family, including a sharp parity right-angle exception and nontrivial nonuniform limiting angle law with a closed elementary-logarithmic CDF. Its contrast with the odd-cycle edge-simplex sine law has an exact geometric explanation through the boundary conditions of the incidence Gram inverse; neither combinatorial simplicity nor known matrix inversion alone gives this geometric and probabilistic classification.
